criteria.remark: Two images across two pages carry no alternative text of any kind, so a screen reader has nothing to announce in their place: the large hero graphic on the home page and the profile avatar on the account page. A reader should take this as evidence that at least some meaningful images on these pages are silent to people who do not see them, and that image alternatives need checking wherever images appear.

Sixteen in-page "skip" style links across five pages were measured by pressing Enter and looking for the destination: in each case no element on the page had the id or name the link points to, such as "main-content" or "news", so activating the link moves no one anywhere. The scan can measure only that. A person has to decide whether another mechanism bypasses the same blocks — a heading, a landmark or a collapsible block. skip-link-works could not look on 1 of 37 scans (the path is replayed once for each rule, and this rule needed its end loaded again); what it would have found is not shown.

Eighteen links across six pages have no text a screen reader can announce. Each contains only a small decorative graphic that is hidden from assistive technology, with no label or title supplying words, so the link is reached by keyboard but announced with nothing to identify where it goes — the social and share links in the page footers are typical. A reader should take this as evidence that the purpose of these links is unavailable to screen reader users.

One form field on one page, the date of birth input on the application form, was flagged because more than one label element is associated with it. What was measured is the multiple association itself; a person has to decide the rest: "Multiple label elements is not widely supported in assistive technologies. Ensure the first label contains all necessary information." Nothing here was determined automatically.

criteria.remark: The VPAT® template answers this criterion itself: the September 2023 errata make it always satisfied under WCAG 2.0 and 2.1, and WCAG 2.2 removed it as obsolete. MANTA did not evaluate it.

Twenty controls across six pages are presented to assistive technology without a name, so nothing identifies them when a screen reader reaches them. They fall into two kinds: links whose only content is a decorative graphic hidden from assistive technology, and form controls with no label at all, including a Social Security number text field and a household size dropdown on the application form. A reader should take this as evidence that these controls cannot be identified non-visually.

Three elements across three pages show the same problem: a "Pending" status badge whose light orange text on a white background measures 2.27:1, well under the 4.5:1 ratio expected for text at that size and weight, which can make the status wording hard to read for people with low vision. One further element on these pages was flagged for a person to judge rather than measured to a conclusion.

Eight form controls across two pages, including the name, date of birth, Social Security number and household size fields on the application form, were measured for the visibility of their focus indicator: the yellow outline shown on focus sits at 1.66:1 against the white surface behind it, below the 3:1 level. That measurement is all the scan establishes. A person has to decide whether another visual cue identifies the focus.
